summary: Outlines a set of goals for new IPv6 site-multihoming architectures, where a site connects through more than one provider. It admits the goals are ambitious and may conflict, so a solution may satisfy only some. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A multihomed site connects to more than one Internet provider, often to keep connectivity when a provider fails. RFC 3582 lists goals for IPv6 solutions and notes that some goals may conflict.

questions: what goals does ipv6 multihoming need
why can multihoming increase routing state
subtitle: Goals for IPv6 sites that connect to more than one transit provider.

tldr.problem: Multihomed sites want redundancy and traffic control, but current IPv4 practices add site-specific routes to the global routing system.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists capabilities and additional requirements for IPv6 multihoming architectures, including scalability, session continuity, manageable operation and security.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3582 is an Informational requirements document, not a proposed solution. It recognizes that some goals may conflict and a design may meet only some of them.

today: RFC 3582 is an Informational document published in August 2003, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It sets goals for IPv6 multihoming architectures rather than defining a solution.

sections.title: The Multihoming Problem
sections.content:
A site is an organization that runs its own Internet Protocol (IP) network and chooses its addressing and routing policy. A transit provider connects such sites to the Internet; a multihomed site has more than one transit provider.

The RFC explains that IPv4 multihoming can cause a site's address block to appear as a separate route even when a larger provider route covers it. The resulting growth adds pressure to the global inter-provider routing system.
sections.plainLanguage: A multihomed site connects to the Internet through more than one provider. The RFC asks how IPv6 can support that choice without adding unreasonable routing state.

sections.title: Capabilities to Preserve
sections.content:
An IPv6 multihoming architecture should support redundancy when a provider or connection fails, and allow a site to share traffic across providers. The RFC also lists performance and policy goals so a site can avoid unwanted paths or choose a provider for business reasons.

Other goals include operational simplicity, continued transport sessions during re-homing, compatibility with DNS behavior and the ability to filter packets with forged source addresses. A transition between provider arrangements is called re-homing.
sections.plainLanguage: A solution should let a site use backup connections and distribute traffic across providers. It should also avoid breaking active sessions when the site's connections change.

sections.title: Scale and Fit Existing Networks
sections.content:
The architecture should support orders of magnitude more multihomed sites without unreasonable demands on the routing system. Router changes should be minor or separate from existing functions, and routers using the changes should still interoperate with ones that do not.

A host that works in a single-homed IPv6 site should continue to work in a multihomed site, even if it does not gain the multihoming benefits. Any interaction between hosts and routing systems should be simple, scalable and secure; site operators should be able to configure and monitor the system.
sections.plainLanguage: The solution should support far more multihomed sites without overwhelming routers. Basic hosts and routers should continue to work even if they do not support the new features.

sections.title: Security Requirements and Trade-Offs
sections.content:
The RFC says multihoming should not make a site more vulnerable than traditional IPv4 multihoming. Routing changes for multihoming should also not make sites that are not multihomed easier to attack.

The abstract cautions that the goals are ambitious and some may conflict. The document defines goals for later designs; it does not specify a multihoming mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: A multihoming design should preserve security for both multihomed and other sites. The RFC does not promise that one design can meet every listed goal.
